notes.b: Physical activity runs on a continuum, from healthy-lifestyle activity to competing to win. The other concepts describe its settings and purposes.
points: Physical activity: any bodily movement produced by skeletal muscles that uses energy. Examples: a walk to school; a professional match.

Play: spontaneous, freely chosen activity done for its own sake, with flexible or self-made rules, mainly associated with children. Examples: chasing games in a playground; kicking a ball around a park with self-made goals.
Leisure and recreation: activity chosen in free time for enjoyment, relaxation and wellbeing, with little emphasis on competition. Examples: a walk; a leisurely cycle.

Physical education: planned, structured learning in, through and about physical activity within the school curriculum, taught by a qualified teacher. Examples: a PE class learning the technique of a striking action; a lesson on how the body responds to exercise.

Mass-participation sports: organised events in which large numbers of people of mixed ability take part at the same time, usually for personal challenge or charity rather than to win. Examples: city marathons; parkrun.
Outdoor and adventure activities: activities in the natural environment that involve challenge, managed risk and uncertainty.
Land-based outdoor and adventure activities: hill walking, orienteering, rock-climbing and mountain biking.
Water-based outdoor and adventure activities: canoeing, kayaking, sailing and surfing.

Sport: organised, competitive physical activity governed by formal rules and a governing body, with an emphasis on performance and winning. Examples: a club league in Gaelic football; a national championship in swimming.

notes.h: Benefits by life stage: children and adolescents
points: Children: motor-skill development, such as running, jumping, throwing and catching.
Children: healthy growth, supported by play and daily activity.
Children: social skills learned through play with others.
Adolescents: self-esteem and body image, which are formed during the teenage years.
Adolescents: stress relief during the pressures of school and exams.
Adolescents: friendships and belonging to a peer group.
Adolescents: lifelong habits that can carry into adult life.

notes.h: Benefits by life stage: adults and older adults
points: Adults: weight and disease prevention, which protects health across working life.
Adults: stress relief from work and family demands.
Adults: social contact outside work.
Adults: work productivity, which keeps people able to meet job demands.
Older adults: balance and strength, which help prevent falls.
Older adults: bone density, which helps protect against fractures.
Older adults: independence in daily life for longer.
Older adults: social contact and reduced loneliness.
Older adults: cognitive health, including thinking and memory.

notes.b: Get Ireland Active sets the national activity guidelines.
points: Children and young people: at least 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity every day.
Adults: at least 30 minutes of moderate activity on five days a week, which is 150 minutes a week.
Older adults: the adult target of 30 minutes of moderate activity on five days a week, plus balance and strength activities.

questions.prompt: Discuss the personal benefits of physical activity for health and wellbeing for people at two different life stages.
questions.model: Adolescents: physical benefits include a lower risk of heart disease and better fitness, and activity helps build lifelong habits that can carry into adulthood. Mental benefits include improved mood, higher self-esteem and relief from the stress of school and exams, which matters most in the teenage years. Friendships and a sense of belonging through team and club activity also support wellbeing at this stage. Older adults: physical benefits include balance and strength that help prevent falls, bone density that helps protect against fractures, and independence in daily life for longer. Mental benefits include reduced stress and anxiety, fewer symptoms of depression and better concentration, while social contact reduces isolation and loneliness and supports cognitive health. The emphasis differs between the stages: for teenagers, self-esteem, body image and habit formation matter most, while for older adults the focus shifts to preventing falls, protecting bone health and staying independent.

questions.prompt: Discuss two economic benefits of physical activity participation.
questions.model: Lower healthcare costs: regular activity reduces the need for treatment for conditions such as heart disease and type 2 diabetes, so the state spends less on healthcare. For the individual, a free activity such as walking costs less than health treatment. Employment and income: the sport and leisure industry employs coaches, instructors and event staff, and events and tourism bring money into an area. Volunteering also keeps clubs running without wage costs. Fewer sick days and higher productivity at work further reduce the cost of absence for employers and the wider economy.

questions.prompt: Explain the concepts 'play' and 'mass-participation sports', giving an example of each.
questions.model: Play is spontaneous, freely chosen activity done for its own sake, with flexible or self-made rules, and is mainly associated with children. Example: chasing games in a playground, where the children change the rules as they go. Mass-participation sports are organised events in which large numbers of people of mixed ability take part at the same time, usually for a personal challenge or charity rather than to win. Example: a city marathon, where runners of all abilities complete the same course together.
